sources.title: Gang of Dragon developer Nagoshi Studio shutters months after NetEase cut funding
sources.text: Studio was "officially dissolved by a shareholders' resolution" on October 31, 2026 Gang of Dragon developer Nagoshi Studio has been closed after NetEase withdrew funding earlier this year. According to Gematsu , the Japanese government gazette Kanpo published a closure notice on October 31, stating the studio was "officially dissolved by a shareholders' resolution." Yakuza series creator Toshihiro Nagoshi founded Nagoshi Studio under NetEase Games in 2022 . In December 2025, the studio debuted a teaser trailer for its new IP, Gang of Dragon, at The Game Awards. By March 2026, NetEase confirmed it had cut funding to the studio but did not disclose reasons or exit terms. Reports indicated NetEase estimated "at least ¥7 billion ($44.4 million) more would be needed" for Nagoshi Studio to complete Gang of Dragon. The developer reportedly "tried to find new sponsors without success" and NetEase told it that "while it is free to continue on its own, it must bear the corresponding costs if it wants to keep the assets or brand." Nagoshi joined Sega in 1989 and spent several years in the AM2 arcade division. He later served as chief creative officer at Sega until 2021, after stepping down from the board . Nagoshi continued at Sega as creative director and was also general director of Like a Dragon developer Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio. Nagoshi Studio is not the only Japanese developer to have ended its partnership with NetEase. In September, Romeo is a Dead Man Grasshopper Manufacture split from the China-based publisher to become independent . CEO Goichi 'Suda51' Suda said the studio "found a strong desire to deliver titles in an even wider variety of styles to video game lovers everywhere," which led it to become independent again. "This decision was reached after thorough discussions with NetEase Games and with their generous cooperation. We continue to cherish the amazing relationship our companies have built, and look forward to further collaboration when the opportunity arises."

sources.title: Nagoshi Studio shuts down
sources.text: Nagoshi Studio , the Shinjuku, Tokyo-based developer founded by Yakuza series creator Toshiro Nagoshi under NetEase Games in November 2021, was officially dissolved by a shareholders’ resolution on October 31, according to a notice published in today’s Japanese government gazette Kanpo . In December 2025, Nagoshi Studio announced GANG OF DRAGON , a Kabukicho-set action adventure game starring Korean actor Ma Dong-seok (Don Lee). In March 2026, Bloomberg reported that NetEase Games planned to cut funding from the studio in May, and that it had the option to go independent if it was able to pay its way out.

sources.title: Yakuza creator's Nagoshi Studio shuts down less than a year after the reveal of Gang of Dragon
sources.text: NetEase reportedly pulled funding earlier this year Nagoshi Studio – the developer founded by Yakuza and Super Monkey Ball creator Toshihiro Nagoshi – has been shut down. Following the release of series semi-reboot Yakuza: Like a Dragon and Lost Judgement, Nagoshi departed Sega after an over 30-year career at the company, founding Nagoshi Studio alongside Yakuza series director Daisuke Sato. The NetEase studio remained pretty quiet until The Game Awards in 2025 where its debut title Gang of Dragon was unveiled with a trailer starring Train to Busan and soon-to-be Physint star Ma Dong-seok. Earlier this year, reports emerged that NetEase was pulling funding on the game after reportedly discovering it would need an extra 7 billion yen in funding, following the developer's YouTube channel and website being taken down, as well as Sato changing his Twitter bio to say ex-Nagoshi Studio, leaving the game and studio's future in doubt. Now, just over five years since Nagoshi left Sega, a notice posted in Japanese government gazette Kanpo (via Gematsu ) confirms that Nagoshi Studio was dissolved on October 31. NetEase has been pulling back on investments over the last year or two, with Worlds Untold – founded by Mass Effect writer Mac Walters – and Jar of Sparks – founded by former Halo lead Jerry Hooks – having their funding pulled. Meanwhile, Suda 51-founded Grasshopper Manufacture self-published its most recent title – Romeo Is a Dead Man – despite being owned by NetEase, with the studio splitting from the publisher to go independent just over a month ago. Neither Nagoshi or the studio has been active on social media since the start of the year, so no official word has been made by the developer. sources.title: Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase
sources.text: Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project. Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo . The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up. The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner , and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year . Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one. Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

sources.title: Nintendo Reveals Development Team Behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake
sources.text: Nintendo has revealed the development team responsible for creating The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . The Super Mario Bros. company typically keeps its cards pretty close to its chest when it comes to the behind-the-scenes details for its biggest releases. The Legend of Zelda series is no exception, but Nintendo did offer a peek behind the curtain as part of an Ocarina of Time remake installment in its Ask the Developer Q&A series. Fans have speculated who might be behind the Nintendo Switch 2 reimagining of an all-time classic since it was announced. While some believed Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft might be leading the charge, for example, the interview confirmed that it's actually Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EDP) Production Group No. 3 that's responsible for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. Featured in the first interview chapter are franchise producer Eiji Aonuma and series directing veteran Hidemaro Fujibayashi, with EDP Production Group No. 3's HokWai Ng, Aya Shida, Hiroki Taguchi, and Masato Ohashi also listed as interviewees to be featured in future highlights. In other words, the core team behind one of the most highly-anticipated games of the last few years is the same group behind most The Legend of Zelda projects from the last 30 years. Longtime fans of the original Nintendo 64 game (or even its 2011 Nintendo 3DS remake) who have feared the Switch 2 version of the story could tarnish its reputation can probably rest easy knowing it was in experienced hands. That said, it is always possible another team like Monolith Soft could have chipped in as a support developer, though we likely won't know the full list of team members until we have a better look at those credits in a few days. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches for Switch 2 November 5. Although it was made by the same hands that have helped keep the classic fantasy franchise kicking for decades, that doesn't mean the developers weren't willing to experiment where they could. During the interview, Aonuma explained that he tried to "basically let the developers make whatever changes they genuinely felt were necessary." "I wanted the team to make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time their own, and to follow through on their own ideas about what the game should be," he added. "That said, I did deliver my fair share of lectures along the way. (Laughs) I took a step back to observe how the younger members of the development team would reimagine The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using the insights and answers they had arrived at on their own." Fujibayashi added that, from his point of view, it was important for the team to have a clear outline for what would and wouldn't be changed from the Nintendo 64 game early on. "For people like us, who know both the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and the recent 3D Legend of Zelda games, there's no shortage of things we’d like to say when it comes to designing a game," he said. "(Laughs) That’s why I took a step back and supported the team from a broader perspective by helping them clarify the things they needed to be mindful of when designing the game." Despite having a good plan for how Nintendo and EDP Production Group No. 3 would tackle The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake from the get-go, Aonuma recently admitted that he's still a bit nervous to see how fans will respond . sources.title: Nintendo Explains Why It Chose to Do Another The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake
sources.text: Nintendo has explained why it chose to develop another The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . Franchise producer Eiji Aonuma was asked what sparked the team's desire to return to one of the most treasured stories in gaming history during the first installment in a series of Ask the Developer Q&A posts. It's an in-depth chat about what it was like to revisit a classic game for Nintendo Switch 2, and how it came about in the first place. The reimagining set to launch in just a few short days will mark the second time Nintendo has remade The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (the first launched for the Nintendo 3DS in 2011 ). Aonuma explained that there were a number of factors Entertainment Planning & Development (EDP) Production Group No. 3 had in mind, with its 40th anniversary being one of the most important. "This year marks the 40th anniversary of the very first Legend of Zelda game," Aonuma said. "With that in mind, I was thinking about what I should create as the producer of the series. Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles. That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'" Aonuma makes a good point. Although he worked on the original Nintendo 64 game when it launched in 1998 and has carried that experience through subsequent entries in the series in the decades since, there are plenty of team members who don't have that same familiarity with its past. Sure, there are those with a passing familiarity with the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time or those who have at least played it, but Aonuma started to wonder how they'd interpret the game "as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games." Allowing them to not only revisit that original story but also leave their own stamp on it, he believes, could help bolster whatever new The Legend of Zelda games come next. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake," he added, "it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development. If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again." Aonuma elaborated, saying that there were many elements considered when choosing to develop a The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2. The team wanted players who had grown used to the open structure of games like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom to enjoy the fun of "progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story" that is "gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way." Nintendo's latest The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches for Switch 2 November 5. Despite having decades of experience and solid reasoning backing the decision to do a remake, Aonuma recently said he's still "nervous" to see what players think . While we wait to get our hands on the launch build, you can see what IGN thought in our hands-on preview . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Added Fast Travel Before Devs Decided It Never Needed It in the First Place
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma asked the Ocarina of Time remake team to add fast travel warp points throughout Hyrule, but it didn't take long for him to realize that was probably a bad idea. Aonuma, one of the franchise's most experienced developers, touched on the trashed concept as part of an Ask the Developer interview shared by Nintendo today. The Nintendo Switch 2 version of one of the most influential video games of all time already seems to have made a few changes to its gameplay formula, but there's one change that he said was better left on the cutting room floor. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time players and speedrunners have spent who knows how much time making Link forward roll to quickly cross great distances. When looking back at how the series has evolved with entries like Breath of the Wild, Aonuma said he found room for improvement, pointing to the wide-open (and iconic) Hyrule Field as one location that might benefit from a fast-travel option. It sounds like it didn't take too long to realize that maybe Nintendo got it right the first time around, though. "So I asked the team to add warp points that didn’t exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts," he explained. "But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what’s this?' "Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again. (Laughs)" That's not to say Nintendo didn't find room to experiment with the structure of Link's first real 3D adventure. Although, for example, the development team intentionally chose to keep loading screens to preserve the feeling of entering a new area, we already know that Link will be able to move faster thanks to a sprint feature. Players can also now take advantage of a dedicated jump button. What might sound like negligible adjustments to some might be earth-shaking changes for others, but we'll have to wait to see just how different The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2 is from the original. "Looking at what they ultimately created, I’m impressed by how rich an experience they were able to craft from a game that first came out 28 years ago," Aonuma added. "At the beginning of development, I remember thinking, 'They could be making more changes.' But as the project went on, it really came across just how deeply this development team cared about the original game, far more than we had imagined." IGN gathered a list of 40 changes we noticed after getting a better look at the remake in September. We then took a closer look with a preview of our own . sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Devs Tried Adding Even More Fast Travel Points, But That Sucked
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out this week, and by all accounts we’ve heard so far, it seems like a pretty faithful remake, albeit with a lot of (necessary, in my opinion) technical and mechanical smoothing out from the original. I don’t envy the devs working on this one (which we now know to be Nintendo EPD): Ocarina of Time is a classic that everyone has really, really strong feelings about. Deciding what to change and what not to change must have been a huge headache. Which is why I’m so, so glad that Eiji Aonuma backtracked on his own ridiculous idea to add a bunch of new fast-travel points Â to this game. This came up during an Ask the Developer interview published by Nintendo today. Now, the original Ocarina of Time already has some fast travel, in that Link can eventually learn ocarina songs that will warp him to each of five of the game’s major dungeons, plus the Temple of Time. And honestly, that’s quite enough to be getting on with, thanks. One of these songs is actually necessary to even access its associated dungeon in the first place, as you need child Link at the Desert Colossus, but he can’t get into Gerudo Valley without being adult Link and riding Epona. But at one point in the remake’s development, longtime Zelda producer and franchise steward Eiji Aonuma thought this wasn’t enough. As Aonuma explains, he observed that a lot of players tried to move around the world faster in the original by spamming Link’s dodge roll, which led him to think there may need to be a faster way to get around the world. I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didnât exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, âWait, whatâs this?â Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren’t working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again. (Laughs) Honestly, what a relief. He’s spot on, really. I played Ocarina of Time for the first time back in January, and while there were times when I was grateful to have a quick way to get from, say, Zora’s Domain all the way back to Castle Town without hoofing it through multiple loading zones I’ve seen a dozen times before, a lot of my favorite discoveries in this game came from being forced to hike around and trip over interesting things. There are all sorts of hidden bits in Hyruleâheart pieces, rupees, goofy little characters. I also just don’t know where you’d even put more fast travel points. I guess I can imagine Aonuma wanting to add warp points to places like Kokiri Forest, Lon Lon Ranch, Zora’s Domain, and other major spots. But if you did that, then why would you ever need to even be in Hyrule Field? Ocarina of Time is not a massive game! It does not take that long to cross Hyrule Field, especially on Epona! It’s pretty easy to get to all those spots from the temple warps! Kids these days don’t want to go on long walks through grassy, Peahat-ridden plains anymore! Mostly I just think it’s funny that Aonuma both proposed this idea and ultimately rejected it. Elsewhere in the interview, Aonuma talks about how the development of this remake involved handing off this old classic to individuals who had never played it until they were put on the project and letting them make their own decisions about how much to alter: If the producers say, âThis is how it should be,â the team would naturally feel obligated to do it that way. So I basically let the developers make whatever changes they genuinely felt were necessary. I wanted the team to make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time their own, and to follow through on their own ideas about what the game should be. That said, I did deliver my fair share of lectures along the way. (Laughs) I took a step back to observe how the younger members of the development team would reimagine The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using the insights and answers they had arrived at on their own. The remake of Ocarina of Time is out later this week, on November 5, and a second part of this Ask the Developer interview is dropping tomorrow. You should read the entirety of it when you get the chance, as it’s pretty neat, though it’s left me desperately wanting to hear whatever “bright and upbeat” piece of music Kondo originally composed for Ganondorf’s theme way back in the ’90s. sources.title: Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"
sources.text: "I thought we needed to address this in this new version." The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty , for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel. In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old. "In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said. "I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again." There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives. Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development." As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style , art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake .

sources.title: Por que Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time é um dos melhores jogos de todos os tempos? Entenda
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time chegou ao mundo no Nintendo 64 há quase 30 anos, em novembro de 1998. Nessa época, do meio para o final dos anos 1990, vimos o lançamento de diversos outros jogos extremamente icônicos, como Final Fantasy 7, Super Mario 64, Half-Life, Metal Gear Solid e Grand Theft Auto, mas Ocarina of Time sempre foi colocado em um patamar separado. Citado por tantos anos como o melhor jogo já criado, é normal questionar o que exatamente torna esse título tão especial e diferente de tantos games que também moldaram e inspiraram a indústria atual. Essa é uma dúvida ainda maior para aqueles que não o jogaram em sua época original e hoje não entendem o motivo dele ser visto dessa forma. Responder isso não é tão simples, mas faremos o possível para explicar o contexto da época de seu lançamento, o que ele trouxe de inovador e o que ele representa para o mundo dos games até hoje. Se quiser entender por que The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time é um dos melhores jogos de todos os tempos, é só conferir logo abaixo! É comum jogar The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hoje em dia pela primeira e achá-lo um bom game, porém normal e sem nada demais que justificasse tantos elogios e adoração da indústria por tanto tempo. Esse sentimento pode se extrapolar para quem o vê no topo do Metacritic com uma nota praticamente impossível de alcançar (99), até para os jogos tidos como obras-primas do meio. Se olhar as avaliações de usuários mais recentes por lá, verá muitos comentários negativos de pessoas falando que o jogo é datado, que os controles são ruins, que a câmera é horrível e que os gráficos são feios, só para citar alguns exemplos. É claro que jogar algo lançado há quase três décadas pela primeira vez pode causar um estranhamento e, obviamente, sempre podemos avaliar como o jogo envelheceu desde sua estreia. Ainda assim, não seria justo fazer um tipo de revisionismo completo, ignorando o contexto do game em seu lançamento e o que ele representou e continua a representar para os games atuais. É além do óbvio observar que o visual, os controles e design de Ocarina of Time são datados em comparação com algo como Elden Ring, The Witcher 3 ou Red Dead Redemption 2. Seria impossível que isso não acontecesse, mas é necessário lembrar que esses jogos não seriam o que são se esse clássico não tivesse existido. Muito do que vemos em jogos de ação e aventura em mundos 3D veio dos pilares estabelecidos nesta era do Nintendo 64 e PlayStation, especialmente do que foi popularizado na aventura de Link. As clássicas perspectivas de lado ou de cima para baixo deram lugar a um ponto de vista em primeira e em terceira pessoa, com a possibilidade de explorar os ambientes à nossa volta com uma sensação de maior liberdade e imersão do que antes. O problema é que essa mudança trazia alguns desafios, já que o jogador teria que cuidar não só da movimentação de seu personagem, como da câmera e ajustes de mira durante combates ou resolução de puzzles. Nos primeiros jogos dessa época, vimos inúmeras tentativas frustradas e, francamente, ruins de entregar uma experiência nova que funcionasse no novo esquema. De muitas formas, Super Mario 64 abriu as portas para algo agradável, que funcionava bem e não era difícil para os jogadores aprenderem. Pouco tempo depois, Ocarina of Time chegaria não só para aprimorar o gameplay tridimensional, mas também para inová-lo. A Nintendo decidiu não dar uma câmera totalmente livre ao jogador, até porque o controle do Nintendo 64 só possuía um analógico, algo que já era inédito o suficiente para consoles da era. O que recebemos foi uma câmera mais fixa atrás de Link e que poderia ser ajustada com um botão, levando seu ângulo de volta às costas do personagem quando necessário. Para lidar com a mira, a empresa apostou na inovação do Z-Targeting, que consistia de uma trava no inimigo, NPC ou objeto com o qual queríamos interagir. Essa forma de trava de mira e o estilo de combate que tínhamos em Ocarina of Time ficaram como uma herança que vemos até hoje em diversos jogos. É quase impossível jogar Dark Souls, ou a maior parte dos games soulslike, sem perceber que a inspiração direta de Link travando sua mira nos inimigos, levantando seu escudo, desviando dos ataques e analisando o padrão ofensivo de seu adversário antes de deferir seus próprios golpes. É claro que a nova perspectiva também favorecia bastante a exploração, fosse das diversas localidades presentes em Hyrule ou qualquer uma das dungeons do game. Embora não se compare com jogos de mundo aberto da atualidade, Ocarina of Time nos deu o primeiro verdadeiro gostinho de como seria estar solto em um mapa vasto e cheio de detalhes, vilarejos, NPCs e inimigos. Melhor do que deixar tudo liberado de início, o game ainda nos restringia a descobrir cada área e dungeon aos poucos, deixando uma sensação de surpresa de início a fim e que nos recompensava por conseguir um upgrade ou item novo. Para aprimorar ainda mais nossa interação com esse mundo, o game contava com as famosas “ações contextuais”, ou seja, tínhamos um botão que podia realizar inúmeras atividades diferentes dependendo da situação. Desta forma, ao apertar o botão “A” no controle, você poderia abrir uma porta, rolar pelo chão, pegar um objeto (como pedra ou vaso), empurrar blocos, abrir baús, escalar, conversar com NPCs e muito mais. É claro que havia jogos em 2D que já tinham ações diferentes para o mesmo botão, mas Ocarina of Time foi quem passou a mostrar o que poderia ser feito diretamente na tela e popularizou de vez esse tipo de uso contextual. Além disso, o ciclo de dia e noite, as histórias individuais de vários NPCs e a forma como o mundo mudava entre as duas épocas (do Link criança e adolescente) tornava essa Hyrule em algo mais palpável e real do que em jogos prévios da franquia. Embora já tivéssemos visto os diferentes povos e regiões nos outros títulos da série, foi em Ocarina of Time que o lore e a construção de mundo se tornou muito mais robusta. Fin

sources.title: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered fighter guide
sources.text: From grappling mutants to cyborg tanks, discover which kaiju is right for you. With its giant-sized fanbase, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has plenty of players ready to get tooth, nail, and claw stuck into its PlayStation 5 release on November 3. Although it would be understandable that newcomers might feel a little intimidated choosing between 12 world crushing kaiju, each with their own stats, moveset, and special abilities. Never fear – we have the rundown on which colossus matches your playstyle to ensure you’re the true king of the monsters. Ideal for: Players who want to dive straight in. The face which sank a thousand ships. Godzilla is the iconic kaiju who all other kaiju want to be, beat, or be friends with. As the game’s default character, the giant lizard is balanced for newbies and veterans alike, with a high amount of starting health and decent all-round stats. Godzilla also possesses a tail useful enough for a mighty wake-up strike when he’s downed, and some fairly swift claws, so many of his melee combos are effective for beginners. But don’t rely too much on his high-energy pulse – while it’s formidable, the slow charge leaves him open to counters. Similarly, ranged attackers can take advantage of his relatively sluggish projectiles, so close that distance or you’ll be heading back to Monster Island with your giant tail between your legs. Ideal for: Players annoyed at their friend for picking Heisei Godzilla. In terms of film history, Godzilla 2000 is a more modern incarnation of the legendary lizard, reflecting a new era for the new millennium. Although he’s arguably a slightly more vulnerable version of his Heisei predecessor. As a result, while Godzilla 2000 is a bit faster than his kaiju shoto fighter twin, he’s not quite as strong. He’s still fairly well balanced and arguably easier to use than Heisei, so makes for a solid alternative. And his distinctive purple dorsal plates look pretty cool, too. Ideal for: Players who want to control the battlefield. There’s a reason why this fearsome three-headed beast is seen as Godzilla’s archnemesis. Giant wings, gravity beams, and a desire to annihilate humanity, the threat of King Ghidorah should never be taken lightly. Given his monstrous size it shouldn’t be a surprise that the ‘supreme ruler of the cosmos’ isn’t the fastest kaiju on the block, but he’s resilient and a perfect ‘zoning’ character, capable of keeping foes at a distance with a variety of projectiles. His flight is a little limited due to its energy drain, but it’s balanced by a lightning blast that has no charge while airborne. However, despite his colossal wings, Ghidorah’s lack of arms and stubby legs makes him a poor melee fighter. Ideal for: Players who think defense is the best offense. He might look a bit like Godzooky with more spikes, but mutant dinosaur Anguirus is one of Godzilla’s most loyal allies – even if his track record against other kaiju hasn’t been the best in the movies. The Monster Island citizen is fast and aggressive, but his low power and lack of long-range attacks means Anguirus is best utilized as a counter-attack specialist. His block might be on the slow side due to its turning animation, but it actually damages an attacking opponent due to Anguirus’ rear spines. With his high defense and solid grappling skills, this mutant shouldn’t be underestimated. Ideal for: Players who love to hit and run. Given its status as a guardian to the ancient underground civilisation of Seatopia, Megalon is more of an antagonist than an out-and-out villain in Godzilla lore. While not quite as domineering as its colossal rivals, the subterranean kaiju is still capable of putting a hurt on with its drill-like appendages. Megalon’s primary advantage is its tunnelling skill which not only allows it to avoid attacks, but also pop-up and grab opponents. Even though burrowing uses energy, it still makes Megalon a difficult fighter to pin down, especially when used in tandem with its myriad of electricity attacks. On the flip side, Megalon isn’t the most durable of beasts with below average defense. Stick and move, or die. Ideal for: Players wanting to attack with deadly speed. One of the most sadistic fighters to hail from M Space Hunter Nebula, cyborg kaiju Gigan is easily one of Godzilla’s more vicious adversaries. Despite being defeated multiple times, the hook-clawed Gigan just keeps coming back for more. Unsurprisingly, Gigan’s tenacious approach makes him perfect for aggressive rushdown tactics. He’s not only swift, but his teleportation ability gives him incredible range and evasion skills. And those hooks aren’t for decoration either, delivering damage-heavy edged strikes. His Laser Eye is a little unwieldy, and he’s vulnerable to energy attacks, but Gigan remains a versatile option for anyone wanting a decent melee and range mix-up. Ideal for: Players wanting a classic tank character. Known as ‘death incarnate’, everything about Destoroyah is built to intimidate. Giant wings, clawed hands, taloned feet… this mutant crustacean almost has it all. Which is to say, Destoroyah is one of the more powerful creatures in the game with brutal physical assaults and a wide variety of high-damage – and often unblockable – energy attacks that truly make him the perfect mid-range monster. But there’s a cost. Destoroyah’s best abilities are extremely power hungry, so without them he’s potentially ineffective given how painfully slow his movement is. Ideal for: Players wanting speed above all else. sources.title: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered Review
sources.text: The first time I ever saw Japan's most famous kaiju on the big screen was in Godzilla 2000: Millennium. Like any nine-year-old kid, I was obsessed with Big G. I read the Dark Horse comics, and I taped all the movies I could on TV. Things were different then; Godzilla was a big deal, but theatrical releases for Godzilla films were incredibly rare in the States If you saw those movies, it was on TV and they were dubbed or edited versions released under different titles like Godzilla: King of the Monsters or Godzilla vs. The Sea Monster. After Godzilla 2000 underperformed, it took another five years for the series to see a theatrical release in the U.S. – and into that void stomped 2002’s Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee. It was the perfect mix of subject matter (big monsters who were super into professional wrestling), genre (3D fighting game), and time period (licensed games were still, like… a thing). It was the kind of game that could dominate a pizza-filled sleepover weekend or become your personality for an entire summer. One friend’s parents bought it for them, and that copy became communal: a holy thing, carried from place to place. Maybe it’s fitting that it’s back now in the form of Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered, 24 years later. The world (and Godzilla) has changed a lot, but original developer Pipeworks is still at the helm. It somehow feels just as relevant now as it did then, just in different ways, and revisiting it was a joy even removed from the nostalgia. There is no one-to-one equivalent for what Destroy All Monsters Melee is, but the idea is pretty simple: you pick one of 12 monsters from Godzilla’s history (up through Godzilla 2000) – Godzilla, Gigan, Megalon, Ghidorah, etc. – then choose a real-world city or iconic Godzilla location to battle it out in. You’ll fight in classic rubber suit wrestling style while dodging environmental hazards, knocking down buildings, throwing rocks and skyscrapers at each other, and squashing the annoying military forces that really would prefer if you made a mess somewhere else. Last kaiju standing wins. Despite the name, this isn't a straight remaster. You're not just looking at uprezzed models. It looks fantastic while also maintaining the “these are guys in rubber suits drop-kicking each other” vibe that defines the films it’s based on. The audio pulls its weight, too – the soundtrack has the booming authority you'd expect from a Godzilla film, buildings crumble and collapse spectacularly, beam attacks sound powerful and painful, the radio calls from military forces in the area let you know where they’ll be focusing their fire, and the announcer is having a blast. And the monsters, of course, sound like themselves. And yeah, Godzilla makes The Noise, just like you remember, even if it’s your first time here. All of this is held together by a spit-and-duct-tape story that's just there to get you brawling: see, there's this alien race called the Vortaak. They're little green men with funky helmets, straight-from-the-‘50s fashion sense, flying saucers, and more than a little ego. They're here to take over the Earth, and what better way to do it than mind control the frankly absurd number of kaiju that are just hanging around, ready to smash a city at a moment's notice? Unfortunately for them, whichever Monster you pick breaks free of their mind control and decides the Earth is worth saving. Driving off the Vortaak means KOing the other monsters. All in a day's work, really. That's Adventure mode, which is one of several single-player options for you to rearrange cities in. You've also got Destruction for the score chasers, where you have to wreck a city in a time limit, a souped-up Adventure mode for monsters who are at a higher level and have better stats (which you gain from experience you earn as you play certain modes), and Survival, which is exactly what it sounds like. Listen, you can count the number of fighting games with good single-player modes on two hands (and several of those have the words “Soul Calibur” in their titles), but what's on offer here is solid if not spectacular. You only start with four monsters and a few stages unlocked, but Pipeworks has smartly reworked this remaster so you can unlock the rest in pretty much whatever order you like. You just have to meet the requirements, which you do by playing, following rumors, and unlocking research, and you can swap what you're focusing on whenever you like. On the one hand, yeah, it's super satisfying to unlock Ghidorah because it's Ghidorah – as soon as he stops being a silhouette I can't select and starts being a gloriously golden three-headed dragon I can take into battle, some lizard part of my brain gets very happy because I can't wait to fly around and shoot lightning with that sumbitch. On the other hand, it's mad annoying to see Rodan or Ghidorah or Mecha Godzilla in Adventure mode and have the 12-year-old who lives in my head put down his slice of pizza long enough to be like “hell yeah, I wanna play that one” and then realize I can't, especially in multiplayer. Does it give you more reasons to keep playing? Absolutely, and this stuff was part and parcel of the original experience. But man, sometimes you just wanna throw down with your friends without worrying about unlocks, you know? Multiplayer, of course, is really what Destroy All Monsters Melee is designed for, and I'm so happy that Pipeworks has added online play in addition to the returning local options. It even works really well! Most of the matches I played pre-release were smooth, though I did suffer a few disconnects. (Almost all of which happened when I was winning or doing well – I'm not saying my boy Lucas is a fraud or anything, but…) It's here, in the multiplayer, that Destroy All Monsters Melee really shines. People will tell you, naively, that this is a button masher with no depth. These people are foolish and wrong, and if this were a Godzilla movie, they'd got a drama

sources.title: Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered decepciona na acessibilidade, apesar da diversão
sources.text: Lançamentos de games em NOVEMBRO de 2026 - Calendário VOXL Além do aguardado GTA 6, novembro traz remake de Ocarina of Time e mais de 30 jogos. Confira as estreias do mês. Crédito: Voxl Sempre fui um grande fã de kaijus e de toda essa cultura de criaturas e robôs gigantes. Por isso, quando soube que Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee receberia uma versão remasterizada, fiquei bastante empolgado. Sempre tive vontade de jogar esse clássico, lançado originalmente em 2002 para Nintendo GameCube e Xbox, mas nunca tive acesso às plataformas necessárias na época. Agora, mais de duas décadas depois, finalmente tenho a oportunidade de conhecer esse jogo em uma versão voltada para os consoles e computadores atuais. Com a chegada de Godzilla Minus Zero , sequência de Godzilla Minus One prevista para novembro de 2026, o momento também parece propício para resgatar um clássico da porradaria entre monstros gigantes. Afinal, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee tem aquela energia dos jogos que você reúne os primos para jogar, sem compromisso com o realismo ou com uma narrativa complexa, apenas para trocar golpes, destruir cenários e dar boas risadas. É um tipo de diversão descompromissada que não se leva tão a sério — e isso faz parte do seu charme. Desenvolvido originalmente pela Pipeworks Studios, o jogo coloca kaijus conhecidos da franquia em confrontos nos quais prédios e outros elementos do cenário também fazem parte da pancadaria. A versão remasterizada busca preservar essa experiência, atualizando a apresentação visual e levando o combate para plataformas modernas, além de incluir recursos como partidas online. Mas, quando um jogo clássico retorna depois de tantos anos, surge uma questão importante: por que modernizar apenas os gráficos e os recursos técnicos? Relançamentos também são oportunidades para rever aspectos da experiência que vão além da resolução das imagens ou do desempenho. Controles mais flexíveis, opções gráficas ajustáveis e recursos de acessibilidade podem fazer a diferença para que mais pessoas consigam aproveitar um jogo. Isso é especialmente relevante em títulos de ação, nos quais acompanhar vários personagens na tela, identificar ataques em meio a explosões, interpretar informações da interface e executar comandos no momento certo pode representar uma barreira para jogadores com deficiência. É com essa perspectiva que analiso Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered . Além de revisitar um clássico que sempre tive vontade de experimentar, quero entender quais recursos de acessibilidade estão disponíveis nessa nova versão, quais barreiras permanecem e até que ponto o relançamento aproveita a oportunidade de adaptar essa experiência às necessidades de jogadores com deficiência. Afinal, destruir cidades com monstros gigantes pode ser uma diversão para muita gente, mas essa diversão só será realmente acessível quando mais jogadores puderem participar dela. Vale ressaltar que a acessibilidade é uma experiência individual e se aplica de maneira diferente a cada pessoa, de acordo com suas necessidades e características. Portanto, as impressões apresentadas nesta análise partem da minha experiência pessoal como pessoa com baixa visão. Meu objetivo é destacar os recursos de acessibilidade presentes no jogo, explicar como eles podem contribuir para uma experiência mais inclusiva e apontar as barreiras que encontrei durante os testes. Essas observações não pretendem representar a experiência de todas as pessoas com deficiência, mas contribuir para que mais jogadores conheçam as possibilidades e limitações oferecidas pelo título. Aviso de transparência: Esta análise foi realizada com uma chave de acesso antecipado disponibilizada pela equipe de Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered para PS5, antes do lançamento oficial do jogo. O título é desenvolvido pela Pipeworks Studios e publicado pela Atari. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered oferece legendas, mas não permite alterar o tamanho ou personalizar sua apresentação. Também não há opções de legendas ocultas ( closed captions ) que identifiquem sons importantes do ambiente e dos combates, o que pode dificultar o acompanhamento das partidas por jogadores surdos ou com deficiência auditiva. Um dos pontos mais decepcionantes é a falta de opções para personalizar os controles. Mesmo sendo um relançamento para plataformas modernas, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered não oferece remapeamento de comandos nem ajustes mais detalhados para adaptar a jogabilidade às necessidades de cada pessoa. Essa limitação pesa especialmente em um jogo de luta e ação no qual é necessário executar diferentes comandos durante confrontos movimentados. Sem a possibilidade de reorganizar os botões, jogadores com deficiência motora podem encontrar dificuldades para realizar determinadas ações ou simplesmente não conseguir configurar os comandos de uma maneira confortável. A ausência de alternativas também reduz a flexibilidade para quem precisa de uma configuração específica por questões de mobilidade ou coordenação. É frustrante que uma versão remasterizada não aproveite a oportunidade para incluir recursos tão importantes. Atualizar os gráficos e levar o jogo a plataformas atuais não é suficiente para modernizar a experiência quando os controles continuam sem opções básicas de personalização. A vibração do controle pode ser ativada ou desativada, mas esse ajuste pontual está longe de compensar a falta de remapeamento. Nas configurações de áudio, o jogo permite ajustar separadamente o volume da música, dos efeitos sonoros e das vozes dos personagens. sources.title: Com GTA 6 e Zelda, novembro começa como o mês do ‘Barbenheimer’ dos games
sources.text: Lançamentos de games em NOVEMBRO de 2026 - Calendário VOXL Além do aguardado GTA 6, novembro traz remake de Ocarina of Time e mais de 30 jogos. Confira as estreias do mês. Crédito: Voxl O ano de 2026 está bastante movimentado no mercado de games, mas novembro promete ser um dos meses mais marcantes da história recente dos videogames. De um lado, temos Grand Theft Auto 6, um dos lançamentos mais aguardados de todos os tempos e que chega após anos de expectativa e adiamentos. Do outro, a Nintendo prepara o retorno de um dos maiores clássicos da indústria: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, em um remake que promete dividir os holofotes com a aventura da Rockstar. A proximidade entre os dois lançamentos já rendeu comparações com o fenômeno “Barbenheimer”, nome dado ao encontro inesperado entre Barbie e Oppenheimer nos cinemas, em julho de 2023. Na época, os filmes de propostas completamente diferentes transformaram a disputa nas bilheterias em um evento cultural, com espectadores abraçando a ideia de assistir às duas produções. Agora, a indústria dos games tem sua própria versão dessa disputa. Enquanto GTA 6 chega em 19 de novembro, o remake de Ocarina of Time está previsto para 5 de novembro, no começo do mês, colocando duas das franquias mais importantes dos videogames em rota de colisão. No entanto, essa “disputa” pode acabar sendo mais amigável do que o esperado por um motivo importante: o mercado é gigante e os títulos estreiam em plataformas bem diferentes. A comparação com o fenômeno Barbenheimer ganhou ainda mais força depois que o programa Saturday Night Live apresentou uma esquete sobre o confronto durante o quadro Weekend Update. Na brincadeira, os protagonistas dos dois jogos, Jason e Link, aparecem conversando com o apresentador Colin Jost sobre a expectativa em torno dos lançamentos de novembro. Interpretado por Marcello Hernández, Jason representa o lado caótico de GTA 6, descrevendo um dia que envolve fuga da prisão, assalto a banco, roubo de carros e até o sequestro de um Boeing Dreamliner. Já Link, interpretado por Mikey Day, apresenta uma rotina consideravelmente mais tranquila em Hyrule, envolvendo a compra de feijões mágicos e uma música tocada na ocarina. A diferença entre os personagens resume bem a proposta da comparação. Enquanto Jason encerra sua participação prometendo “destruição, caos e sexo”, Link oferece “quebra-cabeças e combate leve” como alternativa para os jogadores. A chegada de GTA 6 tem sido um dos principais fatores de influência no calendário de lançamentos de 2026. Diversas desenvolvedoras e distribuidoras evitaram colocar seus grandes jogos na mesma janela do título da Rockstar, temendo perder espaço e atenção do público para um lançamento que deve movimentar toda a indústria. O impacto já aparece no planejamento de outras empresas. Alguns jogos tiveram suas datas alteradas para fugir da concorrência, enquanto outros projetos foram empurrados para 2027. Afinal, GTA 6 não disputa apenas vendas: o jogo também deve dominar as conversas nas redes sociais, transmissões ao vivo, vídeos e a cobertura especializada durante semanas. Confira 26 minutos de gameplay de GTA 6, que chega em 19 de novembro no PS5 e Xbox Series S/X Olhar Estendido divulgado pela Rockstar Games apresenta detalhes da jogabilidade do aguardado Grand Theft Auto VI. A Nintendo, por outro lado, parece disposta a aproveitar a proximidade com uma estratégia diferente. Em vez de tentar competir diretamente com a Rockstar no mesmo dia, a empresa posicionou Ocarina of Time duas semanas antes do lançamento de GTA 6, apostando na força de uma franquia que atravessa gerações. Com isso, a empresa pode ganhar as atenções dos seus fãs e usuários fieis antes da estreia do aguardado game da Rockstar Games. Afinal, o Switch 2 já possui mais de 23 milhões de unidades vendidas e não receberá GTA 6, abrindo caminho para o sucesso de Zelda na plataforma. O peso de GTA 6 no mercado é difícil de ignorar. O novo capítulo da franquia é apontado por relatos da indústria como o videogame mais caro já produzido e promete levar os jogadores de volta a Vice City, agora integrada ao estado fictício de Leonida. A Rockstar também confirmou que o mapa será aproximadamente duas vezes maior que o de GTA 5, com um nível maior de detalhes. O lançamento também deve ser um acontecimento comercial fora do padrão. Executivos da indústria já projetam que parte dos jogadores poderá até tirar folga do trabalho para aproveitar a estreia, algo que ajuda a dimensionar a expectativa em torno do projeto. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake pode conquistar uma nova geração Testamos o remake de Ocarina of Time e encontramos um clássico renovado, com visuais impressionantes, controles modernos e dublagem em português. Crédito: Estadão O remake de Ocarina of Time, por sua vez, segue outro caminho em busca de sucesso. O jogo aposta na nostalgia e na força de um dos jogos mais importantes da história da Nintendo para ganhar a atenção do público. Lançado originalmente em 1998, o título marcou época ao estabelecer referências para aventuras em três dimensões e permanece entre as experiências mais celebradas da franquia The Legend of Zelda. Agora, a nova versão conta com gráficos renovados e uma experiência mais ampla, segundo as primeiras impressões da mídia especializada, incluindo o VOXL. Enquanto algumas pessoas veem um tom de rivalidade nas redes sociais, o Barbenheimer dos games tem uma particularidade interessante: não parece existir uma disputa direta entre as propostas dos dois jogos. GTA 6 promete um mundo aberto gigantesco, violência, liberdade e uma narrativa criminal, enquanto Zelda oferece exploração, enigmas e fantasia. Não só isso, ainda existe uma separação clara de plataformas que pode beneficiar ambos os games durante o mês de novembro. sources.title: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked
sources.text: Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media. Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media. Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop . Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together, according to Kotaku . Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2 . But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way. The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “ Directed Design Experiments ,” which, according to The Half-Life & Portal Encyclopedia, was a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments. sources.title: Valve's canceled Portal follow-up F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to that 12TB Steam leak and some dedicated fans
sources.text: The prequel was canceled because playtesters were confused about why it didn't have the Portal gun F-Stop – the canceled Valve project that was the original Portal follow-up – has leaked online and is fully playable after being found in the massive Steam leak earlier this year. Back in August 12TB of Steam data from 2003 and 2013 dropped online which featured a ton of builds of Valve titles like Portal 2, Left 4 Dead, and Counter Strike: Global Offensive. This data was apparently "hidden in plain sight, but with no protection whatsoever," and was easily accessible without hacking the whole time, proving to be a treasure trove for Valve fanatics, with early Portal 2 builds featuring bullet time being uncovered. And unless Half Life 2: Episode 3 is found anytime soon, the true holy grail of this leak may have been found. As reported by Kotaku , users in the Valve Cut Content project’s Discord have managed to find the game's source code and map data, meaning that F-Stop is fully playable. YouTube user ToothpasteVixen uploaded the intro to the game – featuring earlier narration from a JK Simmons-less Cave Johnson – which will give you a good idea of the concept for those unaware, but to put it simply, it almost feels like an earlier take on the 2019 puzzle game Superliminal where taking photos allows you to manipulate the environment. F-Stop was one of five projects coming from what Gabe Newell described as "Directed Design Experiments," where Valve's production was shut down for a few months which would have the company's teams participate in what is effectively a massive game jam. F-Stop was one of the standout projects from it, with Newell asking the team behind it to develop it into a prequel to Portal. Ultimately, as per Portal 2 - the Final Hours, the project was canceled after playtesters didn't react entirely positively – namely, questioning why a Portal follow-up did not include the Portal Gun – but now, 15 years after the actual Portal 2 was released and with no sequel in sight, you can play a sort of new Portal experience. Backrooms director posts from Valve's office again, and Portal movie speculation is intensifying. sources.title: Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online
sources.text: Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online. The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit . It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake". Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload . There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style. Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment . Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats. How do you solve a problem like Persona 4 ? At Gamescom, we sat down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about the Persona 4 Remake , and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake.

sources.text: We now have an idea of what a Revelations: Persona remake could look like. There’s a video being passed around on the gaming leaks and rumors subreddit that purportedly contains footage of the first Persona game after it’s been hit with the Atlus remake-ification beam. It’s a short video, entirely in Japanese, that seems to depict a gaggle of teenagers trying to escape what looks like a haunted hospital. As the main character (referred to as “boy with earring”) turns a corner, he’s attacked by a monster and the video cuts to a battle sequence. Surprisingly, it looks like the protagonist from Persona 2 , Tatsuya Suou, makes an appearance in the battle, which also features a character who looks like Eriko Kirishima. Combat itself includes a highly stylized UI centered on the attacking character with options that include “persona,” “gun,” “sword,” “item,” and “defend,” as well as a turn order list and other info. There’s no confirmation that this is real footage from a P1 remake and as of publication time, the Reddit thread and the page where the video link is hosted have not yet been subject to any takedown notices. There’s speculation this video could be a mod or a project that was vibe-coded with AI, but comments throughout the Reddit thread say that if it is fake, it’s incredibly well-done. sources.title: GOG wants to bring back physical games, but it's 'a very, very complicated thing'
sources.text: "You click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario." I remember when I'd get bored as a kid, I'd marvel at the back covers of my older brother's PC game boxes—stuff like Guild Wars: Factions and the original World of Warcraft box, the inner cover of which showed a dwarf thwacking a yeti with that one epic sword that looked like a lightsaber. Even back then, the long switch to digital was underway, seemingly for good. But what if we could go back to the glory days of big, embossed boxes and girthy manuals? That's the "dream" of GOG's senior business development and partnerships manager, Marcin Paczynski, as he recently told Gamesradar . Specifically, he wants to see a world where you "would be able to buy physical versions of [games] on GOG … You go to your shelf on GOG, you click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario." I'm sure most PC gaming diehards would agree that, yes, an option to buy physical games—especially older games in a precarious state with regard to preservation—would be pretty neat. Even if you're the sort to snag DRM-free copies of everything you own, a disc makes a game easier to show off, keep close in the event that your hard drive explodes, or place in the seat across from you at a Michelin star restaurant. The problem for GOG is that physical distribution is basically an entirely different business to running a digital storefront. "Because we are talking about physical media, we need to think about logistics, we need to think about storage," Paczynski said, adding that it's "a very, very complicated thing." But the idea has been on the company's collective mind "for years now," so he's not ruling it out. If you don't want to wait, there's always projects like Big Box Collection that let you print your own facsimiles. Or buy used! sources.title: Suda51 Wants A Now-Independent Grasshopper To Bring Back No More Heroes (And One Of His Earliest Games)
sources.text: Grasshopper Manufacture NetEase No More Heroes Grasshopper Manufacture, now independent of Netease Games as of the beginning of October, has been seeking to define what its trajectory will be without the benefit of that financial backing. Suda51, the studio’s founder, sat down with a number of Japanese outlets to discuss the future of the company, how plans have changed since it went independent, and the future of its No More Heroes series. According to Suda51, one of the biggest shifts that will occur as a result of this independence and lack of financial backing is in the scale of the games the studio will be capable of developing. Under NetEase, the company had promised to develop three large games within 10 years, with February’s Romeo Is a Dead Man being one of these.Â These plans will have to be adapted, he explains in an interview with 4Gamer . âThat was a plan we made based on a promise given to NetEase at the time, so that will have to change,â he said, adding, âAs an independent studio itâs now possible to take on various jobs. I want to not just work on my own titles, but also on various interesting IPs.â Speaking to Famitsu in a separate interview, he even mentions two series heâd love to work with: Mobile Suit Gundam and Marvelâs Deadpool . Suda51 admits that itâs a difficult time to become independent. The company handled promotion and the release of Romeo Is a Dead Man in-house, even though it had initially been planned as a NetEase work. Speaking to 4Gamer , he says promoting the title was a challenge for the studio because of how the industry has evolved in recent years. âRaising awareness for a game is really difficult,â he admits. âThatâs because compared to the old promotion, PR and marketing cycle, this era is completely different. Before, it was a challenge over how many TV commercials you could do, how much you were advertising in magazines or online. But thatâs not the case anymore.â To counter the challenges of advertising in the modern era, the studio hopes to take advantage of the Grasshopper brand to some extent. âWeâve been a studio for around 30 years, and our name has even become recognizable overseas to a point, and Iâve realized that there has to be a way we can use that and make more use of our brand power.â As it looks to the future, the company is examining platforms, including Roblox, as a way to allow it toÂ experiment with ideas, and it’s actively recruiting new members to the team. Earlier this year, to mark the release of Romeo Is a Dead Man , the company held a demo event in Shibuya PARCO, a department store in Tokyo, where it proudly announced that another new game would be releasing this year. While that hasnât come to fruition, Suda51 is insisting this unknown game will be released next year. In his conversation with Famitsu , he was more specific about what he wanted to create next. âI have a few ideas of what to make next, but one thing Iâm thinking about is a game I made while I was still at Human, called Moonlight Syndrome . That was the game that started my career, and from there I made The Silver Case, Flower, Sun and Rain and Killer7 . I really want to channel that idea once again if I can. I think No More Heroes has given many people the impression of Grasshopper as a bright and flashy action game studio, but I want to return to the side of the studio that specializes in the dark, serious, and chaotic ideas that we worked on until Killer7 .â Notably, Moonlight Syndrome , released by Human Entertainment in 1997 for PlayStation, has yet to be officially released overseas. At the very least Suda hopes to make this work an international release at last. And perhaps a return to No More Heroes is also in the cards. Speaking about Marvelous, which owns the No More Heroes IP, he said the company is “very aware [that next year is the 20th anniversary of No More Heroes ], so Iâd love for us to do something to mark the occasion. Iâm hoping to do something special, so please look forward to it. Travis Touchdown is definitely coming back!â Based on these interviews, it seems that the now-independent Grasshopper Manufacture is a studio that wishes to look back, as well as look to the future. While its plans have changed since it first signed with NetEase, it wants to at least stick to the intent it previously had, if not at quite the same scale, while creating things that fans of the studio will enjoy. sources.title: Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days
sources.text: Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold. "Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X . Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released . It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released. Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB ). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword , The Blood of Dawnwalker , and Ace Combat 8 . Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong , 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since , is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch. In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review , Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

sources.title: Phantom Blade Zero has sold 4 million copies in 3 days, with a peak Steam player count of 820,000
sources.text: Clearly Donnie Yen should be in more games The people love a good action RPG. At least that's what the numbers around the launch of Phantom Blade Zero would indicate, since it's managed to shift millions of copies and attract north of 820,000 concurrent players on Steam in its first weekend. Developer and publisher S-Game shared one of these stats on social media, posting a nice big graphic on Twitter announcing that Phantom Blade Zero crossed the four million mark in copies sold in just three days. An impressive turnaround by any metric. "Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" reads the caption. The image notes the Metacritic score of 88 and the Steam review score of 89%. Not too shabby whatsoever. Speaking of Valve 's store, a healthy amount of these players are jumping into the Phantom World on PC. On Steam Charts , the peak concurrent player count sits at 822,361. That immediately places the release among the most popular games currently on the store, outstripping the all-time records of Marvel Rivals and Battlefield 6, and even the 24-hour peaks of stalwarts like PUBG and the omni-present Bongo Cat. At time of writing, nearly 400,000 are playing on the PC marketplace. A healthy, robust audience was ready and waiting for this game, it seems. Drawing on wuxia, a genre of Chinese storytelling that fuses martial arts and fantasy elements, Phantom Blade Zero involves you trying to help an assassin clear his name after he's framed for a murder by the organization he works for. The history Chinese setting looks gorgeous and the martial arts-infused combat seems like a tonne of fun. Donnie Yen is involved, and part of me likes to think he's a driving force behind the emphatic playerbase. We're unlikely to ever get an Ip Man game, but we have this, and it's close enough, in all honesty. sources.title: Xbox Game Pass: por que o sucesso das assinaturas preocupa os estúdios?
sources.text: O Xbox Game Pass mudou a maneira como muitos jogadores consomem videogames. Em vez de comprar cada título individualmente, os assinantes têm acesso a um catálogo que reúne produções independentes e grandes lançamentos. Para o consumidor, a proposta é atraente. Mas, para quem desenvolve e publica jogos, a situação é mais complexa. Afinal, disponibilizar um título em um serviço de assinatura ajuda a conquistar público ou prejudica suas vendas? Essa discussão ganhou força em 2023, quando documentos apresentados pela Microsoft à autoridade britânica de concorrência (CMA), durante a análise da aquisição da Activision Blizzard , revelaram que a empresa identificou uma redução nas vendas de jogos após sua entrada no Game Pass. Segundo os documentos apresentados à CMA, análises internas da Microsoft apontaram uma queda nas vendas de determinados jogos nos 12 meses seguintes à inclusão no serviço. O percentual exato não foi divulgado publicamente. A informação contrasta com declarações anteriores de Phil Spencer, chefe da divisão Xbox , que havia defendido que a presença de jogos no catálogo poderia aumentar sua popularidade e impulsionar as vendas. Entretanto, os dois cenários não são necessariamente incompatíveis. Um jogo pode conquistar novos jogadores e ganhar visibilidade inicialmente, mas registrar menos compras individuais ao longo do tempo. O impacto também depende do tamanho do estúdio, do contrato negociado e do comportamento do público. Para desenvolvedoras independentes, serviços como o Game Pass podem funcionar como uma vitrine. Estar disponível em um catálogo de assinatura permite alcançar jogadores que talvez não comprassem o título separadamente. Por outro lado, existe o risco de parte desse público deixar de adquirir o jogo, especialmente quando ele chega ao serviço no lançamento. O modelo também envolve questões financeiras. Dependendo do acordo, a receita obtida pela desenvolvedora pode compensar a redução nas vendas tradicionais. Em outros casos, a participação pode ser menos vantajosa. Por isso, não existe uma resposta única sobre os benefícios das assinaturas para a indústria. Apesar das discussões, o Game Pass não eliminou a compra tradicional de videogames. Os dois modelos continuam coexistindo, oferecendo diferentes maneiras de acessar os mesmos produtos. Para os jogadores, as assinaturas podem representar economia e a oportunidade de experimentar títulos desconhecidos. Para os estúdios, a decisão exige avaliar alcance, receita e possíveis impactos nas vendas. O debate, portanto, não é simplesmente sobre o Game Pass ser bom ou ruim. A questão é entender se um modelo vantajoso para o consumidor também consegue ser sustentável para quem produz os jogos . E essa resposta pode variar bastante de um lançamento para outro. sources.text: Google is gearing up for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake as much as any of us, it seems, with a nostalgic little Easter egg. For years now, Google has included some fun Easter eggs via its search engine. You can type "Minecraft" into your browser to play a bit of the iconic Mojang game. Or, input "do a barrel roll" and watch your screen flip around. The latest Easter egg from Google offers no exception, acting as a silly (but very welcome) ode to Nintendo's beloved Zelda franchise – simply type in "The Legend of Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time" and see for yourself. A Master Sword will appear, and should you click on it, you'll see it inserted – and then you'll be transported back to 1998, when Nintendo's original Ocarina of Time made its way into the wild, sort of like a pseudo-child Link or something. The old Google font, bright primary colors, and exclamation mark intact, is there, along with the 90s search interface you might recall from way back when. The whimsy is unparalleled, honestly. Over on X , comments see folks agreeing that it's a good bit of fun – and, uh, unsurprisingly wishing that Google's search engine still looked like it did in 1998. As one reads, "Can we just… keep it like that now? Forever." Another adds, "Can we get that Google back?" Sadly, though, I think we're stuck as adult Link in 2026. sources.title: Nintendo Officially Comments on Zelda Remake's Divisive Graphics
sources.text: Link, Zelda, and others have a distinct style to them Nintendo 's upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time looks drastically different from the Nintendo 64 original. That's understandable, given the nearly 28 years that have passed since the first 3D Zelda debuted. Beyond the graphical advancements, however, the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time makes some bold character design choices, some of which have divided longtime Zelda fans . In a new interview with the developers of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, we finally get, we finally get some explanation of why Nintendo made certain aesthetic choices, including the decision to make Link, Zelda, and others look more like puppets than strictly photorealistic people. Nintendo developer Aya Shida, who served as art director on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , said that, "When we first considered how to leverage the capabilities of Nintendo Switch 2 to explore new forms of visual expression, a fairly natural direction seemed to be to create a richly detailed world that felt as though it could truly exist. But our goal wasn't simply to make everything look realistic." Shida noted the contrast between the dark but beautiful setting of Hyrule and the game's colorful, quirky characters in the original game. "I felt that this contrast was what gave The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time its mysterious, almost dreamlike charm," Shida explained. "So for this game, we wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world. Figuring out how to strike the right balance became one of the main themes of the art development." Shida revealed that some of the game's art direction was guided by certain keywords: "a puppet-show feel" and "the analog feel of practical effects films." Those phrases refer to creating "a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds." "We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game," Shida explained. "We began by drawing sketches of Link, Zelda, and the other characters. At the same time, to show the kind of world they would inhabit, we created a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree that looked truly alive, carefully adjusting the lighting and textures. We then presented the concept to Aonuma-san, explaining that we wanted characters like these to blend naturally into a world like this." Longtime Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma weighed in on that choice, highlighting how nostalgia for the original Ocarina of Time played into the remake's visual style. "Back when we were developing the game for Nintendo 64, we thought we were making something cutting-edge for the time," Aonuma said. "We weren't trying to create anything nostalgic. But after all these years, the current development team feels a certain sense of nostalgia when they look back at the original. And their efforts to express that nostalgia led them to an analog, puppet-show-like feel. As one of the original developers, that progression made sense to me." Players will get a chance to immerse themselves in the reimagined Hyrule later this week, when The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives on Nintendo Switch 2.
